ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: medicine
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Herbal, industrial and glitterworld medicine, and how much each one helps
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Herbal for scrapes, industrial for deep wounds, glitterworld for the worst cases.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Medicine multiplies the quality of every tend and the success chance of every surgery, and better medicine multiplies more. A doctor can tend without any, but at a fraction of the effect. Herbal medicine is the only kind a colony can make without research, so even a tribe can keep a stock of it.

li.heading: The three kinds

table.li: Medicine | Potency | Caps tend quality at

li.after: Potency multiplies both tend quality and surgery success, so at 1.00 the multiplier is a straight ×1. Tending with no medicine at all counts as 0.30.

li.heading: Making it
li.text:
Herbal medicine comes from healroot and needs no research. Grow healroot early, especially on a tribal start, and give the sowing to a colonist with Plants 8 or higher.
Industrial medicine is made from herbal medicine, neutroamine and cloth after the Medicine production research, which costs 1,500, or 3,000 on a tribal start. There is also a bulk recipe. Buy industrial medicine whenever a trader has it.

li.heading: Who gets what
li.text: Set medical care for each pawn: the best for colonists, herbal or none for prisoners and animals with minor wounds. Keep a few doses per colonist in reserve, and save glitterworld medicine for surgery in poor conditions and for desperate cases.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: doctors and surgery skill
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How much Medical skill your surgeon needs, and why you want two doctors
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Two doctors means one can treat the other.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Medical skill sets your surgeon's base chance before the bed, medicine and room are counted. A skilled doctor in a clean, lit room with a decent hospital bed reaches the success cap for most operations. Tending raises the skill quickly, so give the work to the same people every time, and never rely on just one.

li.heading: The surgeon's base chance
li.text:
The base chance rises with Medical skill, from 10% at level 0 to 90% at level 10, 100% at level 15 and 110% at level 20. Sources disagree on that curve; another table gives 93% at level 10 and 99% at level 20.
The surgeon's body counts too. Manipulation multiplies the chance directly, so 115% manipulation gives ×1.15. Sight multiplies it up to 100%, with no bonus above.

li.heading: Reaching the cap
li.text:
With a normal-quality hospital bed in a lit, clean room, a doctor of about Medical 8 to 10 reaches the 98% cap for most operations. Without a hospital bed or sterile floor it takes about Medical 11 or more. If you have no hospital beds yet, put off risky surgery until your surgeon reaches Medical 11, or use glitterworld medicine to make up the difference.
Either way, leave surgery, and bionic installs above all, to your highest Medical pawn.

li.heading: Training a second doctor
li.text: Tending a human earns 250 XP with no medicine or herbal medicine, 350 with industrial and 500 with glitterworld. Keep your best doctor's Doctor work at priority 1, and train a second doctor alongside. A doctor tending their own wounds works at 70% effectiveness, so when the first one is sick or wounded, someone else should tend them.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: hospital beds
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Better tends, faster immunity and safer surgery
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Any bed can be set to medical. A hospital bed does the job better.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A hospital bed improves tend quality by +10%, speeds up immunity gain ×1.11 and raises surgery success. Its quality matters: a masterwork bed adds far more than an awful one. Set a few beds to "medical" in a clean, lit room and the sick and wounded will be carried there.

li.heading: Quality and surgery

table.li: Quality | Surgery factor | With a vitals monitor

li.after:
Success is still capped at 98%, but the factor climbs with every step, so upgrade to good or better when you can. Sources disagree on the base factor: one gives 1.15 for a hospital bed, another 1.10 (and 1.15 only with a monitor). Ordinary beds and bedrolls have a surgery factor of 1.0; quality multiplies it and material doesn't matter.
Quality also raises rest effectiveness: normal 100%, good 108%, excellent 114%, masterwork 125%, legendary 160%. A sleep accelerator lifts normal to 135%.

li.heading: Setting up the ward
li.text: Mark your hospital beds as medical so the wounded go straight to them, and put them in a clean, well-lit room near the main entrance, so nobody is carried across the base after a raid. Before you can build hospital beds, set ordinary beds to medical in a clean, lit room. The room still counts.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: vitals monitor
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A powered add-on that makes a hospital bed better at everything
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Without power, a vitals monitor is just furniture.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A vitals monitor placed next to a hospital bed links to it and boosts everything the bed already does. It needs power, so it stops in a solar flare and a colony without electricity can't use one. The gains are small, but they apply to every tend and every operation in that bed.

li.heading: What it adds

table.li: Effect | Hospital bed alone | With a monitor

li.after: The surgery factor rises at every other bed quality too.

li.heading: Setting it up
li.text: Place one beside every bed used for surgery or serious illness, then select the bed to check the link line. Each monitor draws 80 W, so keep the hospital on a grid with battery backup to keep the monitors running at night. Without power, make up the difference with a better-quality bed, a clean room and a skilled doctor.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: bleeding and pain
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Tend the bleeder first; pain alone can drop a fighter
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Bleeding wounds first, bruises and cracks later.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Open wounds bleed, and a pawn who loses too much blood dies. Tending stops the bleeding, so after a fight the bleeders come first and the bruises can wait. Pain is the other drain on a fighter: high pain lowers consciousness and can put a pawn down even when no wound is fatal.

li.heading: After a fight
li.text:
The Health tab shows bleeding with an estimate of the time until death. Tend the bleeding wounds first and check that estimate. Any tend stops bleeding, even one without medicine, so if a bleeder's time is short, tend right away with whatever is at hand instead of waiting for medicine. Rescue downed colonists quickly: they keep bleeding while you finish the fight.
Blood on the floor lowers a room's cleanliness and beauty. Clean it out of the hospital before it raises the infection risk for the next patient.

li.heading: Pain
li.text: Infection adds pain as it worsens: +5%, then +8%, +12% and finally +85%. Some drugs cut pain enough to keep a fighter standing:
li.after: Use them only when you must. Every dose carries an addiction risk.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: choosing medicine
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: When herbal is enough, and when to use better medicine
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Most infections are beaten by tending on time, not by the price of the medicine.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Better medicine helps, but surgery success is capped at 98%, so the best medicine is often wasted. Use glitterworld medicine where conditions are poor, industrial for routine surgery, and herbal for infections and minor wounds. For infections, how soon and how often you tend matters as much as what you tend with.

li.heading: Which medicine for which job

table.li: Routine surgery | Industrial, which can already reach the 98% surgery cap
Surgery in poor conditions: a dirty room, a weak bed or a low-skill doctor | Glitterworld
Infections | Herbal or better, with a competent doctor
Prisoners and animals with minor wounds | Herbal
Harvesting organs from someone you don't need to keep alive | Herbal

li.after: Set colonists' default care to industrial medicine, and switch to glitterworld only for a risky operation in a poor room or with a weak surgeon. Check each patient's medical care setting too: patients dying while industrial medicine sits unused is a common mistake.

li.heading: Infections
li.text: A resting colonist with normal immunity gain, treated right away, needs at least 15% average tend quality to survive an infection. Infections need tending about every 12 hours. On a tribal start, herbal medicine handles infections if the tends come on time, so keep the healroot field big enough to keep up.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: infection risk
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Which wounds get infected, and how fast tends and clean rooms prevent it
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Tend fast, and tend indoors on a clean floor.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Many wounds can become infected, and an infection can kill in about a day. The risk depends on the kind of wound, how soon and how well it was tended, and how clean the room is. A quick tend in a clean hospital cuts the risk to a small fraction of the base chance.

li.heading: Base chance by wound

table.li: Missing parts, blunt trauma such as bruises and cracks | None

li.after: Expect infections after animal bites and burns, and check those patients daily.

li.heading: How tending and the room cut it
li.text:
Tending multiplies the chance: ×85% at 0% tend quality, falling evenly to ×5% at 100%. The room multiplies it again: ×50% in a floored room with no filth, ×32% in a clean room with sterile tiles, and ×100% outdoors and in caravans.
So tend every wound fast, ideally in the hospital, keep its floor clean, and lay sterile tiles when you can afford them. On a tribal start, tend indoors on a clean stone floor; it still halves the risk compared with tending outdoors.

li.heading: Timing, and animals
li.text: The infection roll comes after a random delay of 15,000 to 45,000 ticks (6 to 18 hours). Animals are less likely to get infected, but sources disagree on how much: 20% or 10% of a colonist's chance.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: infection and amputation
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The race between infection and immunity, and when to cut
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Severity and immunity both climb. Whichever reaches 100% first decides the outcome.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Once a wound is infected, its severity climbs while the patient builds immunity. If immunity reaches 100% first the patient lives; if severity gets there first, they die. Treatment slows the infection, and amputation is the last resort when a limb is losing the race.

table.li: 87-99% | Extreme | Consciousness capped at 10%, pain +85%, breathing -5%

li.heading: The race
li.text:
Untreated, severity climbs +0.84 a day. Treatment slows it by up to 0.53, so even at 100% treatment it still climbs +0.31 a day. Immunity grows +0.6441 a day while the patient is sick, and once they are immune, severity falls 0.7 a day. Death can come less than 1.19 days after the first symptoms.
At 100% immunity gain speed, immunity takes about 1.55 days. That is too slow to win without treatment unless the speed is 130.4% or more, and pawns with a base immunity gain speed of 39% or less are very vulnerable.
Tend about every 12 hours, with the patient resting in a hospital bed, and compare the severity and immunity bars on the Health tab every few hours. With only herbal medicine, bed rest and tends on time win most of these races on a tribal start.

li.heading: When to amputate
li.text: Amputate before 90% severity. Past 97%, success is very unlikely. If severity on an arm or leg is clearly ahead of immunity, queue the amputation early instead of waiting until just before 90%.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: surgery success
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The formula behind the success chance on every surgery bill
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Even a perfect setup fails 2% of the time.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every surgery's success chance multiplies the surgeon, the bed, the medicine and how hard the operation is. No matter how good the setup, the result is capped at 98%. A failure hurts the patient and wastes the part, so set it up properly before you start.

li.heading: The formula
li.text:
Success = surgeon chance × bed factor × medicine potency × operation multiplier × inspiration, capped at 98%.
Inspiration is ×1 normally and ×2 with an Inspired Surgery. The operation multiplier depends on the job:

li.heading: When it fails
li.text: A failed surgery damages the patient and wastes materials. Failures range from minor through catastrophic to ridiculous. Because of the 98% cap, every surgery that can fail keeps at least a 2% chance of failure.

li.heading: Before you operate
li.text:
Check the success chance on the surgery bill before starting. Use your best doctor, best bed and industrial medicine, and save an inspired surgeon for the riskiest install. Operate in a clean, lit room, since installs are the most sensitive to poor conditions.
Herbal medicine multiplies the chance by 0.6, so on a tribal start save surgery for when it's truly needed.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: operating room conditions
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Clean, lit and indoors: what the room does to surgery odds
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A lamp at the head of the bed does more for surgery than sterile tiles.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The room multiplies the bed's surgery factor. Dirt, darkness and open sky all cut the chance, and the penalties stack. A clean, well-lit room with light at the head of the bed is enough; a sterile floor adds little to surgery but a lot against infection.

li.heading: The room's multipliers

table.li: Clean room with sterile flooring | About ×1.018
Outdoors | Always the 0.6 floor, plus an extra ×0.85
Under 50% light at the head of the bed | A penalty, reaching ×0.75 in complete darkness

li.after: Bionic installs feel these penalties the most. The bed itself starts from a base factor of 1.0 for beds and bedrolls; quality multiplies it and material doesn't matter.

li.heading: Getting the room ready
li.text:
Clean the hospital before surgery and keep a lamp near the head of each bed. Never operate outdoors; move the patient indoors first, even in an emergency. Lay sterile tiles to cut infection risk, even though they add little to surgery itself.
On a tribal start, put a torch lamp by the bed, lay a stone floor and keep it clean, and make sure the room is walled and roofed.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: flu
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The mild disease: bed rest and a tend usually do it
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Most healthy adults beat the flu with bed rest and a tend a day.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Flu is the mildest of the common diseases. Immunity grows almost as fast as severity, so healthy adults often recover with bed rest alone. Tending and a good bed tip the balance for the old and the frail.

li.heading: Getting over it
li.text:
Each day, severity rises +0.249 and immunity +0.239, and treatment at 100% tend quality slows severity by 0.077. While it lasts, flu lowers consciousness, manipulation and breathing by 5% to 20%.
Immunity builds faster when the patient's food is above 12.5%, they rest in a bed (better still a hospital bed or one with a vitals monitor) and their blood filtration is good. So send the patient to bed, keep them fed, and tend daily with herbal medicine or better. Keep a closer eye on elders and anyone with poor blood filtration.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: plague
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Fast and deadly: tend at once and keep the patient in bed
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Plague needs a tend in the first hours, not the first day.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Plague is the fastest killer among the common diseases. Untreated, it kills in about a day and a half, so every patient needs a bed and regular tends from the first hour. Penoxycyline prevents it entirely.

li.heading: How fast it moves
li.text: Each day, severity rises +0.666 and immunity only +0.522. Treatment slows severity by 0.362, which is what lets immunity win. Untreated, plague is lethal in about 1.5 days. The patient is in constant pain of +20% to +85%, and consciousness and manipulation drop by up to 30%.

li.heading: When someone catches it

points.li: Tend immediately with the best medicine you can spare.
Put the patient in a hospital bed and keep them there.
Have a second doctor ready in case the first one catches it.
Without industrial medicine, tend with herbal medicine exactly on time, and keep the doctor close to the patient.

li.after: Penoxycyline prevents plague, so keep it in stock if you can buy or make it.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: malaria
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The tropical disease that weakens the immune system itself
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: In a swamp or rainforest, malaria is the disease you'll see most.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Malaria is common in tropical biomes. It attacks blood filtration and so slows the immunity the patient needs to beat it, which makes it harder to outlast than flu.

li.heading: In the tropics
li.text: In tropical rainforest and swamp, malaria is the most frequent disease, at 17.2% of cases. Penoxycyline prevents it, so on jungle and swamp maps put penoxycyline in the drug policy. Keep a bigger medicine stock there than you would elsewhere.

li.heading: Treating it
li.text: Each day, severity rises +0.370 and immunity +0.314, and treatment slows severity by 0.232. Malaria slows immunity gain by attacking blood filtration, and later stages add pain and reduce consciousness. Put the patient to bed and tend them regularly from the first day.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: sleeping sickness
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Slow and treatable, as long as the patient actually rests
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Sleeping sickness is slow, and bed rest does most of the work.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Sleeping sickness moves slowly and is found only in rainforests and swamps, where it makes up 15.1% of diseases. It is relatively easy to beat if the patient rests, because immunity keeps pace with severity. Left alone, it slowly wears down consciousness. Penoxycyline prevents it.

li.text:
Each day, severity rises +0.12 and immunity +0.11, and treatment slows severity by 0.07. Consciousness and manipulation drop by 2% to 20% while it lasts.
Put the patient to bed and keep them there. Keep the Patient and Bed rest work types at priority 1 for everyone, so the sick actually lie down, and tend regularly; herbal medicine is enough.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: gut worms and muscle parasites
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Chronic pests that need repeated tends, not bed rest
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A colonist with gut worms eats for two.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Gut worms and muscle parasites won't kill anyone, but they won't leave on their own either. There is no immunity race; they're cured once enough tend quality has added up over several tends. Until then they cost food, speed and comfort.

table.li: Effect | Double the hunger rate, +20% pain | Manipulation and movement speed -30%, +20% pain
Cure | 300% total tend quality, or a replaced stomach | 300% total tend quality

li.after: Neither is fatal. Budget extra food for anyone with gut worms.

li.heading: Tending them out
li.text:
300% total tend quality means, for example, four tends at 80%. Each tend lasts 48 hours, so a cure takes days of steady tending. Tend on schedule with the best medicine you can spare, since higher quality means fewer tends. Herbal medicine caps tend quality at 70%, so on a tribal start expect at least five tends.
Bed rest doesn't help, because there is no immunity to build. Let the patient keep working between tends.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: disease risk and penoxycyline
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Which biomes breed which diseases, and the drug that blocks three of them
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Penoxycyline costs 2 neutroamine a dose and never causes addiction.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Diseases arrive as random events, and your biome decides how often and which ones. Tropical maps get them most, deserts and ice the least. Penoxycyline, a cheap drug that never addicts, makes colonists immune to malaria, plague and sleeping sickness while it lasts.

li.heading: How often, by biome
li.after: Difficulty scales the gap between diseases: ×3 on peaceful, ×0.9 on losing is fun. Keep medicine and a free hospital bed ready, especially on swamp and jungle maps.

li.heading: Which diseases
li.text: In temperate forest, flu, plague and malaria each make up 14.9% of cases, and gut worms and muscle parasites 7.5% each. In rainforest and swamp, malaria leads at 17.2%, then sleeping sickness at 15.1%, with flu and plague at 10.8% each. A desert gets flu 18.2% and plague 14.5% of the time, and no malaria.

li.heading: Penoxycyline
li.text:
Penoxycyline prevents malaria, plague and sleeping sickness for about 5.5 days. The disease event still happens, but protected pawns are unaffected. In the tropics, schedule it every 5 days for everyone; a 6-day schedule leaves a gap.
The recipe is 2 neutroamine and 600 ticks of work, and a dose is worth 18 silver. It never causes addiction. Colonies can't produce neutroamine, so buy it from traders whenever you can. Making penoxycyline needs a drug lab, which a tribe has to research first; until then, buy the drug itself from traders.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: prosthetics and bionics
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Replacing lost limbs, and who should do the installing
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Even a peg leg gets a colonist walking again.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A lost leg, hand or eye doesn't have to end a colonist's career. Prosthetics bring back some function, bionics can beat the original, and both need a surgeon. Installing one is a full-difficulty operation, so the doctor, bed and room all count.

points.li: Missing legs and feet. Even a peg leg brings back some movement.

li.heading: The install
li.text: Installing a part uses the 100% operation multiplier, so surgeon skill, bed and room count in full. Let a doctor with Medical 8 or more do the installs, in a clean, lit room with a hospital bed. Bionic arms on the surgeon help with other operations too: they can lift the chance for excising a carcinoma to roughly 90% with normal medicine.

li.heading: Research and cost
li.text: The Prosthetics research costs 600, or 1,200 on a tribal start, and needs Machining first. Since a tribe pays double for the research, buy parts from traders when they turn up. Bionics add to colony wealth, and so to the size of future raids.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: drug policies
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Decide which drugs each colonist may take, and how often
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Scheduled beer helps a colony's mood. Unlimited beer leads to addiction and cirrhosis.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A drug policy decides what each colonist may take, when and why. Turning off "for recreation" and scheduling doses instead keeps the mood boost without the slide into addiction. Set it up once and hand it out in the Assign tab.

li.heading: Setting it up
li.text:
In the Assign tab, open the drug policies. For each drug you want used, turn off "For recreation" and turn on "Scheduled". Keep hard drugs off every policy, except perhaps a separate combat policy for go-juice.
A schedule has a frequency, a maximum mood and a maximum recreation, and all conditions must be met. Most pawns start minor breaks below 35% mood, and walking to the drug takes time, so a mood limit slightly above that works best.

li.heading: Starting schedules
li.text: Common starting points from experienced players:
li.after: In disease-heavy biomes, add penoxycyline every 5 days. On a tribal start, beer and smokeleaf are the drugs you'll have; schedule them the same way.

li.heading: Who ignores the policy
li.text: Pawns with chemical interest or chemical fascination ignore drug policy. Addicted pawns take their drug to satisfy the need by default, even under "No drugs", unless you turn that off in the Assign tab.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: addiction and tolerance
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Each dose can start an addiction, and tolerance builds with every one
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Tolerance builds with every dose, even the scheduled ones.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Each dose of a drug can start an addiction, and each one builds tolerance that weakens the effect and, past certain levels, damages organs. Addiction brings withdrawal: a big mood penalty and stat drops that can tip a pawn into a break. Spaced, scheduled doses keep the risk small.

li.heading: Tolerance
li.text:
Psychite tea, smokeleaf, ambrosia and beer can only start an addiction once tolerance has built up: 10% for psychite tea, 15% for smokeleaf and ambrosia, 25% for beer. Tolerance gain is divided by body size, so big pawns build it more slowly.
High tolerance also does lasting harm. Smokeleaf tolerance above 36% can cause lung carcinoma and above 45% asthma; beer above 45% cirrhosis and carcinoma; psychite drugs above 45% kidney damage. Schedule recreational drugs with gaps instead of allowing them any time, and if a pawn's tolerance climbs, take that drug off their policy for a while. Beer and smokeleaf are the easiest to overuse on a tribal start, so space them like any other drug.
Some tolerance figures differ between sources, so treat them as close guides.

li.heading: Withdrawal
li.text: Withdrawal costs -10 mood for ambrosia and at least -20 for the others, plus stat drops and a higher break risk. A psychite addiction also brings an immediate 15% chance of kidney damage. If someone does get addicted, decide early: keep a steady supply, or ride out withdrawal while the rest of their mood is high.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: beer, smokeleaf, tea and ambrosia
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The soft drugs: what each one does and what it costs to make
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Soft drugs work best in the evening, after the work is done.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The soft drugs give a quick boost to mood and recreation and are easy to make. Used on a schedule, they carry a colony through a bad week, but they shouldn't be its main source of fun. A colony that needs them every day has a bedroom, food or recreation problem that the drugs are hiding: read each colonist's mood thoughts to find what's missing, and fix that first.

li.heading: Side effects
li.text: A joint also brings -30% consciousness, -10% moving, +30% hunger and -20% pain. The consciousness loss slows everything, so schedule joints for the evening, never right before work or a fight. Psychite tea makes rest fall 20% slower and multiplies pain by 0.9. Ambrosia is food too, with 0.20 nutrition.

li.heading: Making them
li.text: Beer is made from 1 wort in 200 ticks and is worth 12 silver. It suits a tribe, because the brewery and fermenting barrel need no electricity. A smokeleaf joint takes 4 smokeleaf leaves and 450 ticks and is worth 11 silver. Psychite tea takes 4 psychoid leaves and 400 ticks at Cooking 2 and is worth 10 silver.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: flake and yayo
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Hard drugs: huge mood, high risk, and no safe dose
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Make flake to sell, not to smoke.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Flake and yayo give an enormous mood boost and fill recreation, which is exactly why they're dangerous. Any dose can cause an overdose, and flake addicts fast. Grow and make them for trade, or not at all.

li.heading: Flake and yayo compared

table.li: Made from | 4 psychoid leaves, 250 ticks | 8 psychoid leaves, 350 ticks

li.after: Yayo is listed at the same +35 mood as flake, which may not be right.

li.heading: Why no dose is safe
li.text:
Every dose of a hard drug carries a 0.5-1.5% chance of an immediate major overdose and adds 0.18-0.35 to overdose severity. There is no safe interval for either, so keep both off every drug policy. If a pawn binges, get a doctor ready for an overdose.
If you grow psychoid, sell the flake and yayo rather than keeping a stockpile at home.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: luciferium
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Large lifelong bonuses, as long as the supply never runs out
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Count the doses before the first one. It's one every 6 days, for life.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Luciferium makes anyone better: sharper, faster, healthier, and it slowly cures scars and chronic illness. It also addicts on the first dose, forever, and you can't make it yourself. Only start if you can guarantee a dose every 6 days for the rest of that colonist's life.

li.heading: What it does
li.text: Luciferium gives +10% consciousness, +5% moving, +15% sight, +70% blood filtration, +20% digestion and +15% blood pumping, and pain ×0.8. It also cures one scar or chronic illness every 15 to 30 days, which makes it worth using on colonists with scars or chronic illnesses you can't fix any other way.

li.heading: The supply
li.text:
It always causes addiction. The need falls 15% a day, so a dose is needed every 6 days, and withdrawal can eventually be fatal. The colony can't produce it; supply comes only from trade and quests.
Count before the first dose: doses in stock ÷ number of users × 6 = days of supply. Then schedule it every 6 days in the drug policy instead of waiting for the need to bite, and send a spare dose with any user who leaves in a caravan.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: go-juice and wake-up
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Combat and work drugs for raids, sieges and emergencies
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: One dose of go-juice lasts 16 hours, long enough for most fights.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Go-juice makes a fighter much better for most of a day; wake-up makes workers faster and keeps them on their feet. Both are made from neutroamine, which colonies can't produce, and both carry an addiction risk. Save them for raids, sieges and emergencies.

li.heading: The two drugs

table.li: Body | +20% consciousness, +50% moving, +35% sight, greatly reduced pain | +10% consciousness, +10% moving, +50% global work speed
Needs | Mood +5, recreation +40%, rest +40% | Rest +100%, recreation +40%
Recipe | 2 neutroamine and 1 yayo, 600 ticks | 2 neutroamine, 900 ticks

li.after: With Royalty, go-juice also gives +15% psyfocus. Wake-up brings a heart attack risk (mean time between 120 days), so keep a doctor nearby after heavy use.

li.heading: Using them
li.text: Dose your fighters at the start of a big raid or a siege assault, not every day, and keep both drugs off recreation in every drug policy. Neutroamine can't be produced by colonies, and a tribe can't make either drug, so buy a few doses from traders for the fights you can't afford to lose.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: overdose
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Stacked doses can put a pawn down, or kill them
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Hard drugs can overdose a pawn on the very first dose.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Overdose builds when a pawn takes too many doses close together, and hard drugs can cause one in a single dose. Below half severity it stays hidden; above it the pawn vomits, then goes down and risks brain damage and death. Severity falls with time, so a bed and patience are the treatment.

li.heading: Severity

table.li: 0.50 to 0.749 | Minor | Consciousness ×50%, vomiting about every 4.8 hours
0.75 to 0.999 | Major | Consciousness capped at 10% and the pawn goes down. A chance of brain chemical damage (on average once per 2.5 days) and of death (once per 3 days)

li.after: Severity drops by 1 per game day.

li.heading: Treating and preventing it
li.text:
Put an overdosed pawn in bed and keep a doctor close until the severity falls below 0.50.
Never stack doses; space them out in the drug policy. Hard drugs carry a 0.5-1.5% chance of an immediate major overdose with every dose, so keep pawns prone to binges away from hard drug stockpiles.
